OVERVIEW

[
1
]

The Plaintiff, Kenneth L. Herman (“
Herman
”)
[1]
is suing the defendant Tanya
Zajdel (“
Zajdel
”). He is seeking a permanent injunction and damages
following an alleged “systemic and unrelenting campaign”, waged by Zajdel, to
destroy his reputation.

[
2
]

Herman claims that Zajdel falsely alleged that he and his friends
drugged and violently gang-raped her.
[2]

[
3
]

He is seeking a permanent injunction enjoining Zajdel to remove all
her postings on social media alleging that Herman drugged her and sexually
assaulted her, to cease disseminating these allegations in any other manner and
to remove her self-published book from circulation and sale.

[
4
]

Zajdel is seeking the dismissal of Herman’s suit. She maintains that
through flashbacks and fragmented memories, she believes that she was drugged
and gang-raped by Herman and at least two of his friends. Subsidiarily, she
states that she had a non-consensual sexual relation with Herman.

[
5
]

Zajdel alleges that the information she published is of public
interest, that it aims to protect potential victims from Herman and his
friends, in addition to allowing “a societal awareness and to free the voice of
the victims of sexual abuse”.
[3]

[
6
]

This case touches on difficult societal issues and the allegations
are horrific.

[
7
]

As recently stated by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Hansman
v.

Neufeld
, “At the core of defamation law are two competing values: freedom
of expression and the protection of reputation. Each is essential to
maintaining a functional democracy.”
[4]

[
8
]

After careful consideration, a thorough review of the oral and
written evidence, the Court concludes that Zajdel published multiple defamatory
statements, knowing them to be false, that destroyed Herman’s reputation.

[
9
]

There is clear and objective evidence that contradicts Zajdel’s
version of events. Zajdel was aware of this clear and objective evidence when
she published her version of events.

[
10
]

Whether or not Zajdel believed her version to be
true after her encounter with Herman, a thorough investigation was conducted by
the police, with her active participation, which clearly revealed that her
recollections do not coincide with what actually happened.

[
11
]

Despite this, and in possession of these
findings, Zajdel posted videos and statements on social media, published a book
in 2020 and an article on Medium, identifying Herman as a sexual predator who
drugged and gang-raped her with his friends and signaling to the public to
beware.

[
12
]

There is no public interest in disseminating a
false story.

[
13
]

For the reasons below, the Court will partially grant
Herman’s Amended Application.

CONTEXT

[
14
]

The following section is lengthy but necessary to
properly understand the context in which the Court is asked to evaluate the
defamatory allegations. The facts as set out in this section are based on the
testimonies given at trial and the exhibits filed in the record.

1.

The Parties

1.1

Plaintiff Herman

[
15
]

Herman is a United States citizen residing in
the State of New York. He is married with two children.

[
16
]

Since graduating from college, Herman evolved in
the technology sector as an entrepreneur. At the time of the alleged defamation
by Zajdel, he was working at Olo, an online ordering business, as Senior VP of
business development.
[5]

1.2

Defendant Zajdel

[
17
]

Zajdel, at the time of relevant events, testified
that she was working as a nurse and residing in the City of Montréal, in the
Province of Québec. She is the mother of two children. She testified that she
now works in trauma treatment, dance therapies and arts treatment.

[
18
]

At trial, Zajdel testified at length, in chief,
on her background and very difficult personal experiences prior to the events
with Herman. Given her emphasis regarding these experiences, the Court sets
them out briefly below.

[
19
]

Zajdel grew up in an ultra orthodox community
that she describes as a “cult”, a segregated community in which men and women
did not interact until the age of 19, after which a marriage was arranged. She
had no interactions with “the opposite sex” except with her father, brother,
and ex-husband.

[
20
]

As a teenager, she met her ex-husband through organized
dates, was engaged and married a few weeks later.

[
21
]

Zajdel testified that her ex-husband was
violent, aggressive, and manipulative. After the marriage, Zajdel states that
she was in a patriarchal system, without access to birth control, and under the
control of men.

[
22
]

She sought help from her parents to no avail. In
her experience, she states that there were no boundaries against domestic
violence and domestic abuse. She testified that her parents were also abusive
at some point in her life.

[
23
]

She recalls that, during her first pregnancy,
her ex-husband assaulted her, while in Israel, by jumping on her stomach in a
fit of rage, causing her to miscarry at six (6) months of gestation.

[
24
]

Zajdel testified that she came back to Montréal,
went on to study at Vanier College, then, at Concordia and McGill universities.

[
25
]

From her union with her ex-husband, she had two
children. She describes her marriage as violent and abusive. Her ex-husband would
choke her and had violent fits of rage. She hid in the bathroom during the fits.

[
26
]

Divorce was not an option because of the risk of
losing her connection to her family. Ultimately, she did seek a divorce after,
according to her testimony, almost being killed by her ex-husband who attempted
to throw her off from a balcony.

[
27
]

Zajdel sought restraining orders to protect
herself and the children. According to evidence filed by Zajdel’s attorneys, her
ex-husband was accused of assault in 2014 and acquitted in 2017.
[6]

[
28
]

Zajdel testified that the events of April 2015
with Herman, followed this difficult period in her life.

[
29
]

She describes herself as a single mother of two
children, going through divorce proceedings and having had no interactions with
men. She describes it as “the start of my journey”.

2.

April
2015 events

[
30
]

The parties met in Montréal in April 2015.

[
31
]

Herman travelled to Montréal to attend a
bachelor party for his friend, Keith Pruzan (“
Pruzan
”). Several other
people, friends and family of the groom, attended the party including Zach
Coopersmith (“
Coopersmith
”).

[7]

[
32
]

Most attendees of the bachelor party were from
out of town and reserved hotel rooms at a hotel in downtown Montréal. Herman
shared a room with Coopersmith.
[8]

2.1

First meeting

[
33
]

On April 9, 2015, Herman met Zajdel for the
first time at a supper club in Old Montréal.

[
34
]

He was accompanied by six to eight friends
including Pruzan, the groom, and Coopersmith. They arrived around 9:30 PM, ate
dinner, after which some tables were cleared to create a dancefloor.

[
35
]

At around 11:30 PM, Herman testified that Zajdel
approached his table with a friend and joked about being able to spot the
bachelor party “a mile away”. Herman offered them drinks and testified that he
and Zajdel started speaking immediately.

[
36
]

At the time of the events, Zajdel testified that
her boyfriend and her roommate had moved out and she was living with a new
roommate, with whom she was going out and learning “about the world”. She had a
babysitter, Hershey Blackman, who watched the kids when she went out.

[
37
]

Zajdel states that she went out with her new
roommate and a friend to the supper club. There, she noticed a table of only men,
including Coopersmith and Herman.

[
38
]

She describes Herman as very well spoken and impressed

[
39
]

Herman states that he was impressed by Zajdel.
They discussed their occupations; he was in the tech industry, and she was a

[
40
]

They enjoyed each other’s company, had many

[
41
]

That night, Zajdel testified that she had difficulty

[
42

[
43

They exchanged phone numbers. On this, Herman

[

That week, the parties exchanged pleasantries by

[9]

[

[

[

[

[

[

[

[

[

[

[

2.3

Departure from the club and arrival at hotel

partialité, la consistance et la cohérence de sa version, la précision de ses

présence ou non d’une raison de mentir n’est généralement pas un facteur
concluant pour évaluer la crédibilité d’un témoin.

[10]
Par ailleurs, le comportement d’un témoin fait partie des éléments
que le Tribunal peut considérer, bien qu’il faille le pondérer avec prudence
puisqu’il n’y a pas de façon standard de réagir lors d’un procès. La question
fondamentale demeurant toujours la fiabilité d’un témoignage. Cela dit, la
sincérité apparente d’un témoin ne garantit pas la véracité de sa version. En
effet, il est connu qu’un témoin peut honnêtement croire que sa version des
faits est véridique, alors qu’il n’en est rien, et ce, tout simplement parce
qu’il se trompe. La crédibilité d’un témoin ne rend donc pas nécessairement son
récit fiable.

- La

fiabilité

[11]
L’évaluation de la fiabilité se réfère à la valeur du récit relaté
par le témoin. Le Tribunal doit rechercher des indices permettant de vérifier
que la version est digne de confiance. La fiabilité d’un témoignage s’entend de
la capacité d’un témoin d’observer, de se remémorer et de relater un fait.

[12]
Le Tribunal doit notamment analyser l’opportunité qu’a eue
le témoin d’acquérir la connaissance des faits qu’il relate, la cohérence et la
vraisemblance de ses propos, les facteurs pouvant influencer sa mémoire, la
vraisemblance de ses propos ainsi que sa façon de communiquer.

[13]
L’intérêt d’un témoin dans l’issue du procès est également un
élément pertinent à prendre en compte, parmi d’autres, dans l’évaluation de son
témoignage. Toutefois, ce facteur ne doit pas peser outre mesure dans l’analyse
de sa crédibilité.

[14]
Par ailleurs, le fait qu’un témoin ne soit pas en mesure de
rapporter tous les événements ne justifie pas automatiquement la mise à l’écart
de tout son témoignage.

-

L’évaluation
de la preuve

[15]
L’évaluation de la version de tout témoin doit se faire au regard
de l’ensemble de la preuve et non sur son seul témoignage. Il est reconnu que
la preuve ne s’apprécie pas en vase clos et que le Tribunal ne doit pas
analyser la preuve de façon morcelée. En outre, l’analyse de la preuve n’est
pas un processus d’élimination successif des éléments de preuve individuels.
Chaque élément doit s’évaluer dans l’ensemble de la preuve, car c’est
l’ensemble de la preuve qui donne à chaque élément sa saveur. Également, dans
son analyse, le Tribunal se doit de considérer toute la preuve, ou l’absence de
preuve, incluant celle qui corrobore la version d’un défendeur. Par ailleurs,
le manque de crédibilité d’un défendeur ou le rejet de sa version n’équivaut
pas à une preuve de sa culpabilité hors de tout doute raisonnable.

SUMMARY
OF FINDINGS

[
453
]

The version of events of Zajdel consist of what
she calls fragmented memories that she has put back together over the days,
weeks and years following the events.

[
454
]

The Court does not consider this to affect her
credibility.

[
455
]

The evidence clearly indicates that apart from
Herman, the rest of the group staying at the hotel arrived around the same time
as the parties exited the elevator into the lobby. Coopersmith and Pruzan could
not have been in the hotel room. Zajdel, in no uncertain terms, systematically
went into explicit and disturbing details about the involvement of these three
people. That night, at the hotel, she was brutally gang raped by several men.
This is her recollection.

[
456
]

Zajdel had the opportunity to investigate her flashbacks
and fragmented memories with the help of the police and her US attorneys. She
was able to obtain clear evidence indicating that her flashbacks and memories do
not reflect what actually happened. She was not brutally gang raped by Herman
and his friends.

[
457
]

Zajdel argues that, if the gang rape did not
happen, then she was still raped by Herman. There is no evidence to support
this. Even her own version of events and memories do not support this
allegation. Her memories are rather of a violent and horrific group assault.

[
458
]

There is no evidence in the court record that a
sexual assault occurred.

[
459
]

Herman was a credible witness. He was forthright
and frank in his testimony, he did not shy away from the any of the details
that cast him in a less favourable light.

[
460
]

The evidence also indicates that, contrary to
what is alleged by Zajdel in her defense, he did not take any legal action
against her as she was vlogging and publicly speaking out against his and his
friends about the alleged gang-rape.

[
461
]

It is only after several years, despite the
police investigations and the communications between the lawyers including
referencing the video footage that clearly contradicts her version of events,
that Herman took legal action. This, after the publication of the book and the Medium
article sent to his employer led to his termination and the terrible toll on
his reputation and well-being.

[
462
]

The explicit details of Zajdel’s allegations are
terrible and distressing. Her persistence in continuing to disseminate them in
the public domain, the Internet, was malicious and intentional.

[
463
]

There is no public interest in disseminating a
false story and it is not Herman’s actions, but Zajdel’s that have a chilling
effect on real victims who have the courage to speak out and seek support and
justice and help other victims.
